text: It is completely unnatural for men to be fathers. So for 25,000 years, we were matriarchy. Patriarchy is fairly new and horrible for everyone, but it's only been around for the last 3,000 years. So when we were a matriarchy, which is the natural state for humanity, the position of men was completely different. There were no fathers. And the idea of monogamy is a made-up patriarchal system because when we were a matriarchy, things were very open and free, and no one knew why women became pregnant. We would just do fertility rituals and be having a good time and be like, oh, these women are pregnant. And then those women would have babies. And nobody cared who the father was, and nobody knew who the father was. Okay, so apparently it is completely unnatural for men to be fathers because humanity spent 25,000 years living in a wonderful matriarchy where nobody knew where babies come from. There were no fathers, no monogamy, no patriarchy, just fertility rituals, complete sexual freedom, and everyone having a good time. Unfortunately, this is not history. This is prehistoric fan fiction. Let's start with the claim that humanity was a matriarchy for 25,000 years. There's absolutely no evidence that human beings lived under one universal matriarchal system for 25,000 years. People were living across completely different continents, climate, and environments. The idea that they all follow the same social system is already ridiculous. She is most likely confusing matriarchy with matrilineal. Matrilineal simply means that family descent or inheritance is traced through the mother's line. It doesn't mean women rule society or dominate men. A matrilineal society can still have male leaders, male warriors, and powerful maternal uncles. So what was the natural state of humanity? The honest answer is that we don't know exactly. We are talking about people who lived tens of thousands of years ago and didn't leave us a written explanation of their gender politics. But based on what we know about hunter-gatherer societies, many of them were probably relatively egalitarian. Men and women often had different roles, but political power and resources were less concentrated than they later became in large agricultural societies. And this is where people make a very convenient switch. Relatively egalitarian does not mean matriarchal. The alternative to men ruling women is not automatically women ruling men. It can also mean that neither sex completely dominates the other. Once agriculture, private property, inheritance, and organized states developed, patriarchal systems became much more common. Land, livestock, and wealth were often passed from fathers to sons. Men dominated armies, governments, religious institutions, and most formal positions of power. So if we generalize across recorded human history, yes, it has been far more patriarchal than matriarchal. That doesn't mean patriarchy appeared everywhere at exactly the same time. It developed differently in different societies. But the claim that it was suddenly invented only 3,000 years ago is simply false. Now let's talk about the idea that there were no fathers. Even in matrilineal societies, fathers exist. Their social role might be different, and the mother's brothers might have more authority over the child, but that doesn't mean men had no relationships with their children. Human children take an incredibly long time to develop and require an enormous amount of food, protection, and care. Fathers helping to provide those things is not some unnatural, patriarchal invention. And no, monogamy was not simply created by patriarchy either. Strict lifelong monogamy has never been universal. Humans have practiced monogamy, serial monogamy, polygyny, and much more rarely, polyandry. But pair bonding between men and women exists across human societies and is far older than modern states or written marriage laws. Finally, her claim that nobody knew why women became pregnant. We obviously cannot ask people who lived 25,000 years ago what they understood about conception. But humans were observing sex, pregnancy, and birth for hundreds of thousands of years. They also watched animals reproduce. Some societies had spiritual beliefs about conception, but believing that spirits or gods are involved doesn't mean people were completely unable to notice that sex and pregnancy were connected. So what is the real conclusion? Human history was diverse. Some societies were matrilineal. Some were relatively egalitarian. Many later societies were strongly patriarchal. But there is no evidence of a universal 25,000-year matriarchy. No evidence that fathers are unnatural and no evidence that humanity spent most of prehistory having fertility rituals while being completely confused about where babies came from. She has taken a few real anthropological concepts, thrown them into a blender, and called the result human history.
